story_text.value:
Hi HN! I just launched gspot. It's a tool that auto detects languages and frameworks you use in a repo and then sets up linters and agent rules.

It handles JS, TS, Python and Swift. You can turn any rule and tool on and off.

You can also create templates from any repo that uses gspot. Templates tell gspot what rules, tools and exceptions to install in a completely different repo. It makes it easy for you to share your linting setup and agent rules.

Feedback would be much appreciated.

title.value: Show HN: Gspot, a tool to lint gstack code

story_text.value:
I wanted my humble Claude on mobile to access my WhatsApp messages but the only options I could find either required WhatsApp Business or an actual server to run Baileys on.

I wanted to run it for free on ClaudeFlare and with my personal WhatsApp account, so I built this.

Important feature - it connects to your Google account as well as WhatsApp to grab the names of all your WhatsApp contacts, otherwise you get only phone numbers for many of them and search doesn't work properly.

This is a single user install because it's both gray area and very private - so point your agent at the repo and let it set things up.

title.value: Show HN: WhatsApp MCP running free on Cloudflare

story_text.value:
I'm a huge fan of an old project called BulletML which was a way of describing shmup (typically bullet hell) patterns in a kinda weird and clunky XML format.

I, however, think sexprs + a little lisp magic can make this idea a lot more fun so I made bullet-script.

You can check out a live repl (ctrl+enter submits the buffer) + demo on the linked site in this submission and you can also check out a language guide here: https://bs.ell.dev/guide/

I'd love to see what you folks can make! If you made a cool pattern please link and share it here!

title.value: Show HN: Bullet Script (bs) – a Lisp(y) VM for shmup bullet patterns

story_text.value:
I enjoy learning new tools watching videos on youtube of people showing their experiments, and sometimes i cannot find a good video explaining exactly what i need.

So i created this project to help me solve that problem.

Creating a video is one prompt, using claude skill to generate the video (@remotion + elevenlabs) and publishing into the page via cloudflare R2

the video script is tested by creating the lab in my local server, all commands/scripts/output is shared in the video page in case i need to verify something or copy the command ran in the video.

the whole project (website+ how to generate a new video) is in github https://github.com/bigzaqui/videolabs

This was my first weekend project with a single Claude Pro subscription, mind blown

title.value: Show HN: Videolabs – narrated terminal-style courses

story_text.value:
Here's a demo video I recorded for a friend that I decided to repost. Sorry for the terrible sound quality and my cough -- hope it's mostly understandable.

https://s3.us-east-2.amazonaws.com/jeffluntgames.com/the-sur...

---

Here's the technical breakdown of what I did:

* Worked with an AI agent (of course) * Described the basic features of the NES * Sprite engine * Input handling * Sound and music

Had the AI build what I'll call a microengine around this. Why do I call it a microengine? Because games on the NES were, I assume, written in assembly, without game engines. But my micro engine (which I named `neo8`) looks like a high-level language, has a basic camera system, and event-based sound system, a polling and event-based input handler that maps inputs to in-game events, a way to model game entities (entity attributes, rendering, animation state machines, etc.), but really just the very basics of what you'd need to create NES-style games on modern hardware.

To be clear, `neo8` is _not_ an emulator. It cannot run NES ROMs. But part of the engine, for the purpose of this demo, involved creating an image, audio, and code structure analysis tool so that I could convert the raw binary data from an actual ROM into .png files, mp3 files, and high-level code.

That high-level code is then compiled to a zero-dependency, native binary, and the little engine supports win/mac/linux as binary outputs.

Anyway, it was fun. Why not just port Contra directly (the "reverse engineer anything" repo, I'm sure could do it direct from the ROM to Rust or something). But I didn't want Contra, because I could just play the real Contra on original hardware or an emulator. Recreating Contra wasn't the point.

The point was to create the engine so I could create new, cross-platform NES-style games using a tiny engine. The Contra demo was simply a proof-of-concept to see if my little engine could replicate Contra's gameplay style, and sure enough it pretty much worked.

title.value: Show HN: I recreated Contra in a custom NES game engine (NOT an emulator)
